newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwean women tell Mrs. Clinton of abuses.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwean women tell Mrs. Clinton of abuses.

text.p: U.S. First Lady Hillary Rodham Clinton on Friday played the role of global feminist, hearing Zimbabwean women tell stories of abuse by men for such things as having bad manners or wearing pants.
Mrs. Clinton was in a familiar role -- listening sympathetically to female concerns -- shortly after her arrival in Zimbabwe on a three-day visit.
Zimbabwe in central Africa was the third country Mrs. Clinton and her 17-year-old daughter Chelsea were visiting on their two-week goodwill mission to six African nations.

At the National Gallery of Art, with brightly coloured paintings on the wall behind her, Mrs. Clinton was guest of honour at a roundtable discussion featuring prominent women from Zimbabwean government, the legal profession, publishing, business and health care.
The message from all was the same -- by and large women in Zimbabwean society are not treated as equal partners with their male counterparts.
They had a supporter in Mrs. Clinton, who has conducted similar sessions on travels around the world.

"A democracy depends on the full integration of women into society, especially on seeing to it that they have equal access to the same tools of opportunity as men: education, health care, and the chance to participate fully in the economy," she said.

Eileen Sawyer, national director of the country's Legal Resources Foundation, said the country has large problems with domestic violence and that some women cited three reasons for being beaten by their husbands: bad manners, wearing pants and trying to mimic the men's functions.
"We need to be taken seriously as women and not be dismissed because of a chauvinistic attitude," she said.

Rudo Karamba, assistance officer of the U.N. High Commission for Refugees, said Zimbabwe's culture would have to change before legal reform could make women more equal, particularly the fact that men are allowed to have two wives.
"As long as you have two wives, it's very difficult to say that a woman should not be abused," she said.
Everjoice Win, a consultant for the Women in Law and Development in Africa organisation, said violence against women is not limited to the poor.

She said in many cases, "People who have been extremely violated in their homes are highly educated women." Oppah Rushesha, deputy minister of information, posts and telecommunications, said Zimbabwe's number of AIDS cases is believed at 1.2 million but that this may be underestimated.
She said women who are infected are considered promiscuous regardless of how they caught the deadly ailment and thus are not given proper care.
Mrs. Clinton said that in her travels she has found that "certainly all of these issues can be found one way or another in every society."
She urged the women to bind together in a show of solidarity to help change Zimbabwe.
"I do hope that there would be a continuing dialogue not only within Africa but around the world so that ... we learn from each other," she told the gathering.
Mrs. Clinton arrived in a light rain and was treated to an airport ceremony featuring young girls in tribal garb dancing to the pounding of drums.
She clapped her hands as a group of youths sang: "Welcome Hillary Clinton, welcome Hillary Clinton, we love the United States."

Moving on to the State House, she shook hands with President Robert Mugabe and air-kissed his wife Grace Mugabe on each cheek. They posed for pictures in front of a fireplace decorated with two crossed spears.
